prompt: In the vocabulary the lesson borrows from `bi-business`, what turns a metric into a KPI?
hint: A metric is any number you can compute. What does a KPI carry besides the number?

choices.text: Its value comes from a DAX measure in the data model rather than from a formula typed in a cell
choices.why: How a number is computed does not make it a KPI. A SUMIFS can produce one as well as a measure can.

choices.text: It is shown on a dashboard that a manager opens every month
choices.why: A dashboard can show plenty of metrics nobody steers by. Being on screen is the result of the choice, not the definition.

choices.text: Somebody chose it to steer by, with a definition, an owner and a comparison
choices.why: Right. Café Serra has hundreds of possible metrics and needs four of them as KPIs.

choices.text: It is expressed as a percentage of something rather than as an amount or a count
choices.why: Revenue in reais is a KPI here and so is the bag count. A KPI can be any kind of number.

prompt: With the timeline on January to June 2026, by how many percent is revenue below the same months of 2025? Give the number with one decimal, without the sign.
A colleague compares January to June 2026 with the whole of 2025 and reports that revenue fell 55.2%. What is wrong with the comparison?
hint: Count the months on each side.

choices.text: Nothing: a fall is a fall, whatever the length of the period
choices.why: The 55.2% is mostly the six months missing from one side. The same months of each year give 10.4%.

choices.text: Six months are set against twelve; the fair comparison is the same months a year earlier
choices.why: Right. Like with like, which is what Revenue LY computes.

choices.text: The percentage should be divided by the 2026 figure, not by 2025's
choices.why: The base is the earlier period, as YoY % has it. The trouble is the length of the periods, not the base.

choices.text: Revenue LY works only when the timeline covers a whole calendar year, January to December
choices.why: It shifts whatever months are selected back one year, which is exactly what fixes this comparison.

prompt: `Products` has a `Unit cost` column. Why does the lesson still leave gross margin off the dashboard?
hint: Ask which year that cost belongs to.

choices.text: Margin needs a relationship between Sales and Products, and the model has none
choices.why: Lesson 15's model relates them through the product code. The relationship is not what is missing.

choices.text: A dashboard must never carry more than four KPIs, or the reader stops reading them
choices.why: Four is what this decision needs, not a rule. The margin is off for a reason about the data.

choices.text: DAX cannot multiply a column by a column from another table
choices.why: It can, with SUMX and RELATED. The formula would work; its answer would be wrong.

choices.text: It holds today's cost only, not 2025's
choices.why: Right. A 2025 margin would be computed with 2026 costs: a number that looks finished and is quietly wrong, so it stays off until there is a cost table with dates.

prompt: Put the three bands of Café Serra's dashboard in order, from the top of the screen to the bottom.
hint: What the reader came for, then why, then where to act.
items: The KPI cards, with last year beside each number
The chart of revenue per month
Revenue by channel and by product
trap: Breakdowns first make the reader assemble the answer from parts before knowing whether there is a problem.

prompt: The KPI row says the half-year is 10.4% down. What does the chart of months add that the cards cannot?
hint: Compare January to March with April to June.

choices.text: When: all of the fall came after March
choices.why: Right. The first quarter grew and the second fell: R$ 12,139 against R$ 9,303, then R$ 3,804 against R$ 8,486: a total of the two looks like a mediocre half-year.

choices.text: The same half-year total, drawn larger for readers who skip the numbers
choices.why: The chart splits the total by month, which is information the total does not carry.

choices.text: Which of the three channels lost the revenue that the cards report
choices.why: That is the breakdown at the bottom. The months say when, the channels say where.

choices.text: A forecast for July to December 2026
choices.why: Nothing on this dashboard forecasts. It compares what happened with the same months of the year before.

prompt: Why does the lesson put the slicer and the timeline at the top of the dashboard?
hint: Where does the eye look for a control, and what does a control near one chart seem to filter?

choices.text: Excel accepts slicers only in the first rows of a sheet
choices.why: A slicer can sit anywhere. The position is about how the reader reads it.

choices.text: Above everything they filter, they read as controls of the whole screen
choices.why: Right. At the bottom they look like part of the last chart and seem to filter only that one.

choices.text: So that they come out on the first page when the dashboard is exported as a PDF
choices.why: The PDF has no slicers that work. The placement is for the person filtering on screen.

choices.text: Because the timeline needs the full width of the sheet
choices.why: It shares the top band with the slicer in the figure. Width is not the reason.

prompt: Which of these follow the lesson's rules for a one-screen dashboard? Choose all that apply.
hint: Every rule is about what the reader sees without effort.

choices.text: Gridlines and headings turned off on the dashboard sheet
choices.why: Right. They help somebody editing cells and are noise for somebody reading.

choices.text: A second half below the first screen, for readers who want detail
choices.why: Most readers never scroll. If it does not fit, it is two dashboards or a chart too many.

choices.text: The sign written in front of every change, as well as its colour
choices.why: Right. Colour alone fails a colour-blind reader and a black-and-white printout.

choices.text: Amounts shown with two decimal places of reais
choices.why: R$ 15,943.00 has two digits nobody needs. Whole reais read faster.

choices.text: Columns of the sheet made narrow and equal, used as the layout grid
choices.why: Right. Cards and charts sized to whole columns line up without effort.

prompt: Why do the four pivot tables live on the `Calc` sheet instead of on the dashboard?
hint: What does a pivot table do when a slicer changes?

choices.text: A pivot from the data model cannot share a sheet with a chart
choices.why: It can. The reason is that it changes size.

choices.text: A hidden sheet refreshes faster than a visible one
choices.why: Hiding changes nothing about refreshing. It only takes the sheet out of view.

choices.text: A pivot changes size as it is filtered
choices.why: Right. On the dashboard it would push into the charts and cards; on a sheet of its own it can change size freely.

choices.text: GETPIVOTDATA reads only pivots that sit on a different sheet from the formula
choices.why: It reads a pivot on any sheet, its own included. Separation is about layout.

prompt: The slicer is on `Wholesale`. The channel chart shows R$ 11,128 for the half-year, and the Revenue card beside it shows R$ 15,943. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: R$ 15,943 is the total of every channel.

choices.text: The `Revenue` measure ignores any filter on `Channel`
choices.why: Measures respond to filters; that is what filter context means. The card's pivot never received this one.

choices.text: `GETPIVOTDATA` returns the grand total of all channels in every case
choices.why: It returns what the pivot holds, and the pivot holds what its filters let through.

choices.text: The chart is reading last year's revenue
choices.why: R$ 11,128 is Wholesale for January to June 2026. Last year's was R$ 13,392.

choices.text: The `KPI` pivot is not ticked in the slicer's Report Connections
choices.why: Right. Each number is correct for what its pivot was told, and the screen contradicts itself.

prompt: Why does the lesson insist on the `GETPIVOTDATA` form instead of a plain `=Calc!B4`?
hint: What happens to B4 when somebody adds a field to the pivot?

choices.text: It finds the value by its name, not by its position
choices.why: Right. A plain reference points at a position, and after a change the card shows whatever moved into it, with no error.

choices.text: It recalculates faster than a plain reference does, in a big workbook
choices.why: Speed is not the difference. The difference shows up the day the pivot changes shape.

choices.text: A plain reference cannot point at a cell on another sheet
choices.why: `=Calc!B4` is a perfectly good reference to another sheet. It just points at a position.

choices.text: It refreshes the pivot before reading from it
choices.why: No formula refreshes a pivot. Refresh All does that.

prompt: With the timeline on January to June 2026 and the slicer on `Wholesale`, what does the Revenue card show, in reais?
hint: The same as the SUMIFS that adds the channel to the dates.

prompt: What does `=COUNTIFS(Sales[Date], ">="&DATE(2026,1,1), Sales[Date], "<"&DATE(2026,7,1))` return on your data?
hint: It counts the sales of the first half of 2026.

prompt: A new slicer filters only the pivot you clicked in. The dialog that connects it to the other pivots is Report ___.
hint: Right-click the slicer.

prompt: The owner wants a second slicer, on `Product`, and wants the cards to follow it. Besides inserting the slicer, what has to be done?
hint: What did the `Channel` slicer need?

choices.text: Nothing: a slicer on the data model filters every pivot built from the model
choices.why: A new slicer is connected only to the pivot you clicked in, whatever the source.

choices.text: Rewrite each `GETPIVOTDATA` formula to name the product
choices.why: The formula reads whatever the KPI pivot holds. Once the pivot is filtered, the formula follows.

choices.text: Tick all four pivots in its Report Connections, as for the `Channel` slicer
choices.why: Right. Every control has to reach every pivot, or the screen contradicts itself.

choices.text: Add `Product` to the rows of the `KPI` pivot
choices.why: That would split each value into six, and the GETPIVOTDATA formulas would still read the grand total, unfiltered.

prompt: In `=HYPERLINK("#Dashboard!A1", "Dashboard")`, what does the `#` tell Excel?
hint: Where does the link go?

choices.text: That the address is a place in this workbook
choices.why: Right. What follows the # is an ordinary address, and clicking the cell jumps to it.

choices.text: That the link opens in a web browser
choices.why: Without the #, the text would be read as a file or a web address. The # keeps it inside the workbook.

choices.text: That `Dashboard` is a defined name rather than a sheet
choices.why: Here it is followed by a sheet and a cell. The # says where to look, not what kind of name follows.

choices.text: That the cell shows a number instead of text
choices.why: The second argument decides what the cell shows: the word Dashboard.

prompt: You rename the `Sales` sheet to `Sales data`. What happens to `=HYPERLINK("#Sales!A1", "Sales")` on `Contents`?
hint: Is the address a reference or a piece of text?

choices.text: Excel rewrites the text inside the quotes, as it does for references
choices.why: References follow a rename; text in quotes never does. This address is text.

choices.text: It stops working, since the address is only text
choices.why: Right. Rename sheets before writing the links, or check every link after a rename.

choices.text: It jumps to cell A1 of whichever sheet is first
choices.why: It has no fallback. The place it names no longer exists.

choices.text: It keeps working until the file is closed and opened again
choices.why: Nothing about the link changes on reopening. It points at a sheet that no longer exists from the moment of the rename.

prompt: You protect the `Dashboard` sheet, and now the slicer will not filter. Which step was missed?
hint: The slicer is an object on a protected sheet.

choices.text: Hiding the `Calc` sheet first
choices.why: Hiding Calc does not affect the slicer, which sits on Dashboard.

choices.text: Freezing the top row
choices.why: Freezing is about scrolling, and the dashboard does not scroll.

choices.text: Encrypting the workbook with a password
choices.why: Encryption decides who can open the file, not what works inside it.

choices.text: Unticking Locked in the slicer's Size and Properties before protecting
choices.why: Right, and ticking Use PivotTable & PivotChart while protecting. Then click the slicer to see that it still filters.

prompt: Match each command to what it does to the workbook.
hint: Two of them keep accidents out; one keeps people out.

pairs.left: View › Freeze Panes › Freeze Top Row
pairs.right: Keeps the headers in view while the rows scroll
Takes a sheet out of view without protecting it
Stops cells from being typed over by accident

pairs.left: File › Info › Protect Workbook › Encrypt with Password
pairs.right: Makes the file unreadable without the password

right_distractors: Refreshes the model every time the file is opened

prompt: The owner wants an employee to see the dashboard's numbers but not the list of customers. What does the lesson recommend?
hint: Where are the customers, and who can read them?

choices.text: Hide the `Customers` sheet before sending the workbook
choices.why: Unhide brings it back, and the customers are in the model as well.

choices.text: Protect every sheet with a password
choices.why: Protection stops typing, not reading. Every row is still in the file.

choices.text: Hide the column that holds the names
choices.why: A hidden column is one right-click from visible, and the model still holds it.

choices.text: Send a PDF of the dashboard, never the workbook itself
choices.why: Right. The PDF carries the numbers and charts and none of the data behind them.

prompt: Why does the lesson clear the slicer before saving the copy that leaves?
hint: What state does a workbook open in?

choices.text: Excel refuses to save a workbook while any of its slicers is filtered
choices.why: It saves happily, and that is the danger: the reader opens a filtered dashboard.

choices.text: A cleared slicer makes the file smaller
choices.why: The file holds the same data either way. The point is what the reader sees first.

choices.text: The workbook opens in the state it was saved in, slicer included
choices.why: Right. Saved on Wholesale, it opens as a dashboard of one channel, with nothing on the cards to say so.

choices.text: Slicers reset on opening anyway; clearing them only saves the reader a click
choices.why: They do not reset. The slicer state is saved with the file.

prompt: After Refresh All, the title still says *data to 23 June 2026*, although the sources now hold sales from July. What does that tell you?
hint: The date in the title is `=MAX(Sales[Date])`.

choices.text: July's sales stay hidden until the timeline is moved to July
choices.why: The title reads the Sales table, not the timeline. A July sale in the table would move it.

choices.text: The new rows never arrived, so every card is out of date too
choices.why: Right. That is exactly what the date is for: it is the one place the screen admits how old it is.

choices.text: MAX ignores dates later than the timeline's last month
choices.why: MAX on the table knows nothing about the timeline.

choices.text: The title is typed text and has to be edited by hand each month
choices.why: It is a formula, so that nobody has to remember to edit it.

prompt: Put the steps before saving the copy that leaves in the lesson's order.
hint: Fresh data first, the default view next, the opening position last.
items: Data › Refresh All, and check the date in the title
Set the timeline to the dashboard's period
Go to Dashboard, select A1 and save
trap: Saving before refreshing sends last month's numbers in a file that looks current.

prompt: With the timeline on January to June 2026 and every channel selected, match each measure to what the dashboard shows.
hint: Revenue LY is the same months of 2025.

prompt: On `Wholesale`, January to June 2026, revenue fell 16.9% while the average sale rose from R$ 893 to R$ 1,236. What happened?
hint: Average sale is revenue divided by the number of sales.

choices.text: Wholesale prices rose by about 38%
choices.why: Prices rose by a few reais a bag in 2026. A 38% rise in the average comes from fewer, bigger sales.

choices.text: Fewer, larger sales: 9 in 2026 against 15 a year earlier
choices.why: Right. Each sale was bigger and there were far fewer of them, so the total fell while the average rose.

choices.text: More bags were sold, in each sale and in total
choices.why: Wholesale sold 100 bags against 153. Bags per sale rose; the total did not.

choices.text: The measure divides by bags, not by sales
choices.why: Average sale is DIVIDE([Revenue], [Sales count]). The rise is in the data, not the measure.

prompt: Which of these belong on Café Serra's dashboard, by the lesson's argument? Choose all that apply.
hint: Each item either serves the owner's decision honestly or it does not.

choices.text: Revenue beside the same months of last year
choices.why: Right. A number with nothing beside it is not a KPI.

choices.text: Gross margin for 2025, computed with today's unit costs
choices.why: It would apply 2026 costs to 2025 sales, and nothing on the screen would say so.

choices.text: A chart of revenue per month, 2025 beside 2026
choices.why: Right. It shows that the whole fall came after March, which no total can.

choices.text: Every sale of the period, in a table under the charts
choices.why: It breaks the one-screen rule and answers no part of the decision. The rows are a click away on Sales.

choices.text: The date of the last sale in the data
choices.why: Right. It is how the reader knows how fresh the screen is.
